hook.text: Every test passes. Two dashboards report revenue for the same twelve orders. One says nineteen hundred forty-nine dollars. The other says forty-five hundred fifty-five.

hook-meaning.text: Neither query errors, and neither looks wrong. Interviews probe exactly this: who defines a number, and the joins that quietly change it.

plan.text: Eighteen questions on metrics and the semantic layer. Eight are worked through, most on the page's own orders in Postgres, and ten come quickly at the end.

disagree.text: Question one. What causes two dashboards to report different numbers for the same metric? Two hand-written definitions.

disagree-how.text: One counts refunds, tax or cancelled orders, and the other doesn't. One goes by order date, the other by ship date. They aggregate at different grains. Or one of them hits a fan trap.

disagree-cure.text: The cure is one shared definition, in a semantic layer or a certified mart, so both dashboards run identical SQL.
disagree-cure.spoken: The cure is one shared definition, in a semantic layer or a certified mart, so both dashboards run identical sequel.

disagree-widen.text: Left alone, the gap grows: each definition weighs a shift in traffic differently, so they drift apart just when everyone is looking.

fan.text: Question two. What is a fan-out join, or fan trap, and why is it dangerous? You join a table to a one-to-many detail table, then sum a measure from the one side.

fan-two.text: Orders one and two are worth a hundred fifty dollars. Order one has three items, order two has one. Join the items, and order one's hundred dollars appears three times: three hundred fifty.

fan-all.text: Across all twelve orders, the join returns twenty-four rows, and nineteen hundred forty-nine dollars becomes forty-five hundred fifty-five, more than double.

fan-danger.text: That's the danger: nothing errors, and the result looks ordinary. Each order is counted once per item, so the bigger the baskets, the bigger the error.

fan-tell.text: The tell is the row count. Twelve orders went into the join, and twenty-four rows came out.

avoid.text: Question three. How do you avoid double counting from a fan-out? Aggregate each grain before you join. Sum revenue from orders alone, units from the items alone, then put the two summaries together.

avoid-run.text: Back to nineteen hundred forty-nine dollars, and thirty-eight units.

avoid-after.text: If you must aggregate after the join, count distinct order IDs, twelve, and sum only measures that live on the item rows, like quantity.

avoid-layer.text: A semantic layer does this for you: it knows each measure's grain, and aggregates before the join fans out.

chasm.text: Question four. What is a chasm trap, and how does it differ from a fan trap? Two independent one-to-many tables meet at one dimension: payments and refunds, both by customer.

chasm-run.text: Ada made three payments, a hundred eighty dollars, and got two refunds, thirty. Join all three, and every payment pairs with every refund: six rows. Payments sum to three hundred sixty, refunds to ninety.

chasm-diff.text: A fan trap inflates one measure. A chasm trap multiplies two many-sides together, so both inflate.

chasm-fix.text: Same fix: total each branch on its own, then join the totals. A hundred eighty, and thirty.

chasm-left.text: Join them to the customer with left joins, though. Ben paid forty dollars and was never refunded, and an inner join drops him.

layer.text: Question five. What is a semantic layer, or metrics layer? A governed, central definition of metrics and dimensions, sitting between your models and the business intelligence, or BI, tools.

layer-once.text: Take the page's completed revenue: the sum of amount, where status is completed. It's defined once. Every tool asks the layer for completed revenue by month or by region, and the layer writes the SQL: the joins, the aggregation, the filter.
layer-once.spoken: Take the page's completed revenue: the sum of amount, where status is completed. It's defined once. Every tool asks the layer for completed revenue by month or by region, and the layer writes the sequel: the joins, the aggregation, the filter.

layer-why.text: It separates what a metric means from how each dashboard computes it.

entities.text: Question six. What are entities, dimensions, and measures in a semantic model? Entities are the join keys, and they set the grain: an order, a customer. Dimensions are what you group and filter by: status, region, date. Measures are what you aggregate: an amount, a count.

entities-run.text: Declared on the page's two tables, they tell the layer that revenue lives on orders and units on items. Ask for both by order, and it sums each at its own grain before it joins: nineteen hundred forty-nine dollars and thirty-eight units, with no fan trap.

nonadd.text: Question seven. Why can't you simply sum pre-aggregated distinct counts or ratios? Because they're non-additive.

nonadd-distinct.text: Store the number of distinct products in each order, then add up those twelve counts: twenty-four. The items table holds seven products. Product A is in five orders, so it's counted five times.

nonadd-users.text: Daily active users summed into a month fail the same way: someone active on two days counts twice. Recount from the rows for the month, or merge distinct-count sketches, small summaries built to combine.

nonadd-ratio.text: Ratios break too. One day converts five of ten sessions, the next twenty of a thousand. Average the two rates, and you get twenty-six percent. Sum the conversions and the sessions, then divide: two point five percent.

nonadd-store.text: So store the numerator and the denominator, which do add up, and divide at the end.

ratio.text: Question eight. How does a semantic layer handle a ratio metric correctly? It keeps the numerator and the denominator as two separate measures, and divides at query time, at whatever grain is asked for. Nothing is pre-divided.

ratio-week.text: Conversion by week sums the week's conversions and sessions first, then divides once, so there's no average of averages.

ratio-limit.text: What it can't do is rescue parts that don't match: a numerator and a denominator with different filters or grains, or a dimension one of them doesn't have.

r-truth.text: Question nine. Why does a single source of truth for metrics matter? Without one, every dashboard and notebook re-implements revenue slightly differently. One definition means one place to change it, the same answer everywhere, and versioned code instead of tribal knowledge.

r-drift.text: Question ten. What is metric drift, and how do you prevent it? It's one metric slowly coming to mean different things in different places, as copies of its logic spread and mutate. Define it once, under version control and review, and point every consumer at that.

r-metricflow.text: Question eleven. What is the dbt Semantic Layer, or MetricFlow? Semantic models and metrics, declared in YAML beside the dbt project. MetricFlow, the layer's query compiler, turns a request for a metric by a dimension into warehouse SQL, and BI tools ask for it through an API.
r-metricflow.spoken: Question eleven. What is the dbt Semantic Layer, or MetricFlow? Semantic models and metrics, declared in yammel beside the dbt project. MetricFlow, the layer's query compiler, turns a request for a metric by a dimension into warehouse sequel, and BI tools ask for it through an API.

r-lookml.text: Question twelve. What is LookML, and how does Looker's semantic layer work? LookML is the modeling language of Looker, a BI tool: dimensions and measures in views, joins in explores. Looker writes the SQL from what a user picks. It was an early, influential semantic layer.
r-lookml.spoken: Question twelve. What is LookML, and how does Looker's semantic layer work? LookML is the modeling language of Looker, a BI tool: dimensions and measures in views, joins in explores. Looker writes the sequel from what a user picks. It was an early, influential semantic layer.

r-measure.text: Question thirteen. What is the difference between a measure and a metric? A measure is a raw aggregate on one table, like the sum of amount. A metric is the business number built from measures, with filters, ratios or time logic, like completed revenue.

r-contains.text: Question fourteen. What does a metric definition contain? The aggregation, the entity and grain it lives on, the dimensions it can be sliced by, its filters, and its time grain. A ratio adds a numerator and a denominator.

r-additive.text: Question fifteen. What is the difference between additive, semi-additive, and non-additive metrics? Revenue sums across everything. An account balance sums across accounts but not across months: take the latest, or the average. Ratios and distinct counts never sum; recompute them from the rows.

r-governance.text: Question sixteen. What is governance in the metrics context? An owner for each metric, code review on every change, certification of the trusted ones, documented meaning and lineage, and access controls.

r-cumulative.text: Question seventeen. What is a cumulative or time-window metric, and why define it centrally? It aggregates over a trailing window, like rolling twenty-eight-day active users, or month-to-date revenue. Windows are easy to get subtly different by hand, so define the grain and the window once.

r-wide.text: Question eighteen. When is a wide, pre-joined mart preferable to querying through a semantic layer? For a heavy BI workload, or a tool that struggles with dynamic joins: reads are fast and predictable. It costs flexibility and storage, and its logic must still come from the governed definitions, or it becomes one more place to drift.

next.text: All of these definitions were written for people reading dashboards. Now the reader is a language model. Next: AI and the semantic layer.
